recipes.reheating: Reheat very gently over low heat — coconut milk can split if overheated.
healthBenefits: Lean fish protein.
Coconut milk provides healthy MCTs.
Lower in calories than meat curries.
recipes.culturalNote: Coconut fish curry is the everyday expression of Swahili coastal cooking — drawing on the two most abundant ingredients of the Indian Ocean coast: fresh fish and coconut milk. It is a dish that tastes like the coast itself.
regionalVariations: Classic Swahili coconut fish curry.
Spicy version with extra chilli.
Coconut fish with green peppers.
Lemon coconut fish — extra citrus.

faqs.q: What fish works best?
faqs.a: Any firm white fish holds up in coconut curry — tilapia, snapper, sea bass, or catfish. Avoid delicate fish that flake apart easily.

recipes.cookingScience: Coconut milk contains emulsified fat droplets stabilised by proteins. Boiling disrupts this emulsion — the fat separates from the water phase, creating a greasy, split sauce. Gentle simmering maintains the emulsion, producing the characteristic creamy, velvety texture.
sustainabilityTips: Choose locally sourced Kenyan fish over imported varieties.
Coconut palms are a perennial crop — coconut milk production has minimal environmental impact.

recipes.title: Kenyan Fish Fingers
recipes.community: Popular in urban Kenyan households — a family favourite
recipes.description: Kenyan Fish Fingers — tilapia or other white fish cut into strips, seasoned with Kenyan spices, coated in spiced breadcrumbs, and deep-fried until golden and crispy. Beloved by children and adults alike — the Kenyan take on a universal classic.
recipes.longDescription: Fish fingers with a Kenyan twist — the familiar breadcrumbed format elevated with garlic, ginger, lemon, and paprika in the coating. Crispy outside, tender and flaky within, they are the ideal introduction to fish for children and a beloved quick meal for the whole family.
ingredients: 600g tilapia or white fish fillets — cut into finger-sized strips
steps: Mix garlic, lemon juice, paprika, cumin, turmeric, salt, and pepper. Toss the fish strips in this seasoning.
Mix the paprika and cumin into the breadcrumbs for a flavoured coating.
Set up a coating station: flour in bowl 1, beaten egg in bowl 2, spiced breadcrumbs in bowl 3.
Coat each fish strip: flour first, then egg, then breadcrumbs. Press gently to adhere.
Heat oil to 175°C.
Fry in batches for 3—4 minutes until deep golden brown, turning once.
Drain on paper towels. Serve immediately.
chefTips: Season the breadcrumbs as well as the fish — this doubles the flavour impact.
Press the breadcrumbs firmly onto the fish — loose coating falls off during frying.
Make sure the oil is hot enough before the fish goes in.
commonMistakes: Wet fish — pat completely dry before coating or the crumb does not adhere.
Too cool oil — produces soggy, pale fish fingers.
Overcrowding — lowers oil temperature.
recipes.storage: Refrigerate for up to 2 days. Freeze uncooked for up to 2 months.
recipes.reheating: Reheat in oven at 190°C for 8 minutes.
healthBenefits: Good source of fish protein.
Homemade version allows control over ingredients.
Fish provides omega-3 fatty acids.
recipes.culturalNote: Fish fingers have become a firm favourite in Kenyan urban households — the familiar format with a distinctly Kenyan spice profile makes them irresistible to children and adults alike.
regionalVariations: Classic Kenyan spiced fish fingers.
Coconut breadcrumb fish fingers — coastal style.
Extra spicy version.

faqs.q: Can I bake these instead of frying?
faqs.a: Yes — place on a lightly oiled baking tray and bake at 200°C for 15—18 minutes, turning halfway. They will not be as crispy as fried but are a lighter option.

recipes.cookingScience: The three-stage coating (flour → egg → breadcrumb) creates a moisture barrier that protects the fish during frying. The flour helps the egg adhere; the egg binds the breadcrumbs; the breadcrumbs create the crispy shell through starch gelatinisation and Maillard browning.
sustainabilityTips: Homemade fish fingers produce no excess packaging and allow you to use any sustainable fish variety.

recipes.title: Kenyan Garlic Butter Fish
recipes.localName: Samaki wa Siagi na Vitunguu Saumu
recipes.community: Popular in urban Kenyan restaurants and households
recipes.description: Kenyan Garlic Butter Fish — tilapia or white fish fillets pan-seared until golden and crispy, then finished with a fragrant garlic butter sauce with lemon, fresh coriander, and a hint of chilli. Simple, luxurious, and ready in under 20 minutes.
recipes.longDescription: Garlic butter fish is the Kenyan kitchen at its most elegant and effortless — a simple pan sauce of butter, garlic, lemon, and coriander transforms a piece of fish into something restaurant-worthy in minutes. It has become a favourite in Nairobi restaurants and urban homes for exactly this reason.
ingredients: 2 tilapia fillets or white fish fillets (about 500g total)
steps: Pat fish dry and season with salt, pepper, and paprika.
Heat oil in a pan over high heat. Add fish fillets skin-side down.
Cook without moving for 3—4 minutes until golden and crispy on the bottom.
Flip carefully. Cook for 2—3 minutes on the other side.
Remove fish and set aside.
Reduce heat to medium. Add butter to the same pan.
When butter is melted and foaming, add garlic and chilli flakes. Cook for 30 seconds until fragrant — do not burn.
Add lemon juice. Swirl to combine.
Return fish to the pan. Spoon the garlic butter sauce over the fish.
Scatter with coriander and serve immediately.
chefTips: A hot pan and dry fish are the secrets to a good sear — no moisture, maximum heat.
Do not move the fish during the first sear — let the crust form naturally.
The garlic butter sauce comes together in under 1 minute — have everything ready before you start.
Brown butter (cook until it turns golden and smells nutty) makes this extraordinary.
commonMistakes: Wet fish — it steams instead of searing.
Burning the garlic — 30 seconds maximum on medium heat.
Moving the fish too early — it tears.
recipes.storage: Best eaten immediately.
recipes.reheating: Not recommended — garlic butter fish is best fresh.
healthBenefits: Very high protein from fish.
Garlic provides allicin with antimicrobial properties.
Lemon adds vitamin C.
recipes.culturalNote: Garlic butter fish represents the contemporary urban Kenyan kitchen — drawing on classic technique with local ingredients to create something that feels both luxurious and accessible.
regionalVariations: Classic garlic butter.
Coconut garlic butter — coastal fusion.
Herb butter fish — with mixed fresh herbs.

faqs.q: What other fish can I use?
faqs.a: Any white fish fillets work beautifully — snapper, sea bass, catfish, or cod. Salmon also works well if available.

recipes.cookingScience: When butter reaches around 150°C it begins to brown (beurre noisette) — the milk solids caramelise through the Maillard reaction, developing a complex, nutty aroma and flavour that plain butter does not have. This is why garlic butter sauce made in a hot pan tastes so much more complex than butter simply melted.
sustainabilityTips: Use locally sourced Kenyan fish whenever possible.

recipes.title: Kenyan Prawn Curry
recipes.community: Swahili — especially popular in Mombasa and coastal communities
recipes.description: Kenyan Prawn Curry — plump prawns simmered in a fragrant, warmly spiced tomato and onion curry sauce. One of the most luxurious dishes of the Kenyan Swahili coast — ready in under 30 minutes and deeply aromatic.
recipes.longDescription: The Indian Ocean coastline of Kenya has always been prawn territory — fresh prawns from the warm coastal waters have been a prized ingredient in Swahili cooking for centuries. Mombasa's prawn curry, fragrant with garlic, ginger, and coastal spices, is one of the most celebrated dishes of the coast. It cooks astonishingly quickly — prawns need only minutes — making it one of the fastest premium meals in the Kenyan repertoire.
ingredients: 500g large prawns — peeled and deveined, tails on
steps: Season prawns with salt, turmeric, and paprika.
Cook onions in oil until golden — 8 minutes.
Add garlic and ginger. Cook 1 minute.
Add tomatoes. Cook for 6—8 minutes until thick.
Add curry powder, cumin, and remaining spices. Stir 1 minute.
Add water. Bring to a gentle simmer.
Add prawns. Cook for 3—5 minutes only — until prawns are pink and just cooked through.
Stir in garam masala and lemon juice.
Scatter with coriander. Serve immediately with rice.
chefTips: Prawns cook in 3—5 minutes maximum — the most common mistake is overcooking them to rubbery toughness.
Build the curry sauce fully before adding prawns — they will finish cooking in the residual heat.
Prawns are done when they have curled into a C-shape and turned fully pink. An O-shape means overcooked.
commonMistakes: Overcooking prawns — they turn rubbery and tough in minutes.
Adding prawns to a cold or barely warm sauce — they stew rather than cook cleanly.
recipes.storage: Best eaten immediately. Do not reheat prawns — they overcook easily.
recipes.reheating: Not recommended — serve prawn curry fresh.
healthBenefits: Prawns are very high in protein and low in fat.
Excellent source of iodine, selenium, and zinc.
Low in calories — one of the leanest protein options in the collection.
recipes.culturalNote: Prawn curry is one of the jewels of Kenyan coastal cuisine — the combination of fresh Indian Ocean prawns and the Swahili-Indian spice tradition produces one of East Africa's most celebrated dishes. In Mombasa's restaurants, prawn curry with coconut rice is the quintessential coastal meal.
regionalVariations: Classic Swahili prawn curry.
Coconut prawn curry — with coconut milk for richness.
Dry prawn curry — sauce reduced to a coating.
Spicy prawn curry with extra chilli.

faqs.q: Can I use frozen prawns?
faqs.a: Yes — thaw completely and pat very dry before using. Wet prawns release water into the curry and dilute the sauce.

faqs.q: What size prawns are best?
faqs.a: Large prawns (16—20 per 500g) give the best eating experience in curry. Small prawns overcook too quickly before the sauce has time to coat them.

recipes.cookingScience: Prawn proteins (primarily myosin) denature and coagulate at around 60°C — extremely quickly. The characteristic curling from straight to C-shape happens as the muscle proteins contract during cooking. A C-shape means perfectly cooked; an O-shape means the protein has contracted further — the prawn is overcooked and will be rubbery.
sustainabilityTips: Buy locally sourced Kenyan prawns from the Indian Ocean coast when possible — they are fresher and more sustainably harvested than imported frozen prawns.

recipes.title: Kenyan Coconut Prawns
recipes.community: Swahili — a coastal celebration dish
recipes.description: Kenyan Coconut Prawns — fresh prawns cooked in a creamy, fragrant coconut milk sauce with garlic, ginger, tomatoes, and Swahili coastal spices. The most luxurious quick dish of the Kenyan coast — ready in 20 minutes and tasting like a celebration.
recipes.longDescription: Uduvi wa Nazi brings together two of the Kenyan coast's greatest ingredients — fresh Indian Ocean prawns and thick coconut milk — in a dish that is simultaneously elegant and effortless. The coconut milk creates a naturally sweet, creamy sauce that envelops the prawns without overwhelming their delicate flavour. Served with coconut rice, it is the coastal celebration meal at its most irresistible.
ingredients: 500g large prawns — peeled and deveined, tails on
½ tsp sugar — optional, to balance the coconut
steps: Season prawns with salt, turmeric, and paprika.
Cook onions in oil over medium heat until soft and golden — 6 minutes.
Add garlic and ginger. Cook 30 seconds.
Add tomatoes. Cook for 5—6 minutes until softened.
Add curry powder and remaining spices. Stir 30 seconds.
Pour in coconut milk. Stir gently. Bring to a gentle simmer — do not boil hard.
Add prawns. Cook for 3—5 minutes until pink and just cooked through.
Add lemon juice, sugar if using, and coriander.
Serve immediately with coconut rice.
chefTips: Never boil the coconut milk hard — it splits. A gentle simmer is the key.
Do not overcook the prawns — 3—5 minutes maximum.
A pinch of sugar balances the coconut milk beautifully without making the dish sweet.
commonMistakes: Boiling the coconut milk vigorously — it separates into oil and water.
Overcooking prawns — rubbery and tough.

relatedDish.note: KEN080 (Coconut Prawns) and KEN079 (Prawn Curry) are both Swahili coastal prawn dishes. Prawn curry uses a tomato-based sauce; coconut prawns replaces the tomato base with coconut milk for a creamier, sweeter, more fragrant result. Both are quick and luxurious — the coconut version is the more celebratory of the two.

recipes.storage: Best eaten immediately.
recipes.reheating: Not recommended.
healthBenefits: Very lean, high-protein prawns.
Coconut milk provides healthy MCTs.
Garlic and ginger add antioxidant benefits.
recipes.culturalNote: Coconut prawns represent the pinnacle of everyday Swahili coastal cooking — two abundant coastal ingredients (prawns from the Indian Ocean, coconuts from the palm-lined shore) combined in a dish that is both quick and celebratory. In Mombasa, this dish symbolises the generosity and warmth of coastal Kenyan hospitality.
regionalVariations: Classic coconut prawns.
Spicy coconut prawns with extra chilli.
Coconut prawns with vegetables.
Dry coconut prawns — sauce reduced to a glaze.

faqs.q: Can I use shrimp instead of prawns?
faqs.a: Yes — large shrimp work well. Reduce cooking time to 2—3 minutes as they are smaller and cook faster.

recipes.cookingScience: The fat in coconut milk coats the prawn proteins and helps them retain moisture during brief cooking. The emulsified structure of coconut milk also creates a naturally thick, creamy sauce without any thickening agents — provided it is not boiled hard, which breaks the emulsion.
sustainabilityTips: Source prawns from local Kenyan coastal fisheries when possible.
Choose coconut milk from sustainably grown coconut palms.

recipes.title: Kenyan Managu
recipes.community: Kikuyu, Luhya, Luo, Kisii — enjoyed across Kenya
recipes.description: Managu — African Nightshade — is one of Kenya's most nutritious indigenous vegetables. The slightly bitter leaves are sautéed with onions, tomatoes, garlic, and optional milk until tender and deeply flavourful. A traditional Kenyan side dish with remarkable health benefits.
recipes.longDescription: Managu is not for the timid — its gentle bitterness is part of its identity, a flavour that older generations associate with nourishment and health. Cooked properly with onions and tomatoes, the bitterness mellows to a pleasant earthiness, and the dish develops a silky quality from the natural mucilage in the leaves. Eaten with ugali, it is one of the most complete traditional Kenyan meals.
ingredients: 500g fresh managu leaves — washed and roughly chopped
½ cup milk — optional, for creamier flavour

substitutions.alternative: Spinach — milder flavour without the bitterness
Coconut milk for a coastal variation

steps: Wash the managu leaves thoroughly in several changes of water. Remove any tough stems.
Blanch in boiling water for 2 minutes, then drain — this reduces the bitterness significantly.
Heat oil in a pan over medium heat. Cook onions until soft — 5 minutes.
Add garlic. Cook 30 seconds.
Add tomatoes. Cook for 5—6 minutes until softened.
Add the blanched managu leaves and water. Stir to combine.
Cover and cook for 8—10 minutes until the leaves are completely tender.
Add milk if using. Season with salt and pepper. Simmer 3 minutes.
Serve hot with ugali.
chefTips: Blanching before cooking is the key step — it significantly reduces the bitterness.
Milk added at the end creates a creamier, richer version that many families prefer.
Do not overcook — the leaves should retain some structure.
commonMistakes: Skipping the blanching step — the dish can be unpleasantly bitter.
Overcooking — the leaves lose colour and texture.

heritage.origin: Indigenous to East African highlands — cultivated and wild-harvested for centuries
heritage.history: Managu (African nightshade, Solanum nigrum) is one of the oldest and most nutritious indigenous vegetables in Kenya. It has been gathered from homestead gardens and wild patches across the country for generations, prized for its distinctive slightly bitter flavour that mellows with cooking and for its exceptional nutritional density.
heritage.modernEvolution: Once considered a wild weed in some communities, managu has seen a revival as interest in indigenous vegetables grows among health-conscious urban Kenyans.

recipes.storage: Best eaten fresh. Refrigerate for up to 2 days.
recipes.reheating: Warm gently over low heat.
healthBenefits: Extremely rich in iron — one of the highest plant-based iron sources in East African cuisine.
High in calcium and vitamin A.
Contains antioxidants and anti-inflammatory compounds.
Very low in calories — just 75 kcal per serving.
recipes.culturalNote: Managu is deeply woven into the food culture of Kenya's farming communities. It grows wild in many homestead gardens and has sustained generations of Kenyan families as an accessible, nutritious vegetable available throughout the year.
regionalVariations: Classic managu with tomatoes.
Managu with milk — creamier version.
Managu with groundnuts — peanut paste stirred in.
Mixed managu and terere.

faqs.q: Is African nightshade safe to eat?
faqs.a: Yes — the cultivated and semi-wild varieties of Solanum nigrum used in Kenyan cooking are safe when cooked. Cooking neutralises the small amounts of solanine present in raw leaves. Always cook before eating.

faqs.q: Where can I find managu?
faqs.a: In Kenya, managu is available in most local markets. Outside Kenya, it may be found in African grocery stores as "African nightshade" or in Asian markets as "black nightshade".

recipes.cookingScience: The bitter compounds in managu are primarily glycoalkaloids (principally solanine), which are water-soluble and heat-sensitive. Blanching in boiling water extracts a significant proportion of these compounds into the blanching water, which is then discarded — dramatically reducing the bitterness while preserving the nutritional benefits.
sustainabilityTips: Managu grows readily in Kenyan gardens with minimal water and inputs.
It can be harvested continuously by picking outer leaves and allowing the plant to continue growing.

recipes.title: Kenyan Pumpkin Leaves
recipes.community: Enjoyed across all Kenyan communities
recipes.description: Kenyan Pumpkin Leaves — the tender young leaves of the pumpkin plant sautéed with onions, tomatoes, and garlic into a silky, mildly flavoured vegetable dish. One of Kenya's most underrated traditional greens — sweet, mild, and deeply nourishing.
recipes.longDescription: Where sukuma wiki and managu are well-known, pumpkin leaves remain one of the quiet treasures of Kenyan home cooking. The tender young tendrils and leaves of the pumpkin plant — harvested before the fruit develops — have a mild, slightly sweet flavour and a silky texture when cooked. In many Kenyan homesteads, the pumpkin plant serves double duty: fruit for eating and leaves for cooking.
ingredients: 500g fresh pumpkin leaves and tender stems — washed
steps: Wash the pumpkin leaves thoroughly. Remove any fibrous stems — only tender stems are edible.
If the stems are fibrous, strip the outer fibre by pulling from the base.
Heat oil in a pan. Cook onions until soft — 5 minutes.
Add garlic. Cook 30 seconds.
Add tomatoes. Cook for 5 minutes until softened.
Add pumpkin leaves and water. Stir to combine.
Cover and cook for 6—8 minutes until the leaves are wilted and tender.
Season with salt and pepper. Serve immediately.
chefTips: Only use the tender young leaves and thin stems — older leaves are fibrous and tough.
Pumpkin leaves have a natural silkiness — this is normal and desirable.
A splash of cream or milk added at the end creates a luxurious variation.
commonMistakes: Using tough mature leaves — they remain fibrous even after cooking.
Overcooking — the leaves lose their pleasant silky texture.
recipes.storage: Best eaten fresh. Refrigerate for up to 2 days.
recipes.reheating: Warm gently over low heat.
healthBenefits: Rich in iron and calcium.
High in beta-carotene (vitamin A).
Good source of folate and vitamin C.
Very low in calories.
recipes.culturalNote: Pumpkin leaves are one of the most resourceful vegetables in Kenyan cooking — grown as a by-product of pumpkin cultivation in homestead gardens, they provide nutrition during the growing season before the pumpkins are harvested.
regionalVariations: Classic pumpkin leaves with tomatoes.
Pumpkin leaves with milk.
Mixed pumpkin leaves and managu.
Coconut pumpkin leaves — coastal style.

faqs.q: Can I eat pumpkin leaves?
faqs.a: Yes — the tender young leaves and stems of the pumpkin plant (Cucurbita species) are edible and nutritious. They are widely eaten in Kenya and across East and West Africa.

recipes.cookingScience: Pumpkin leaves contain mucilage — a natural plant compound that creates a silky texture when the leaves are cooked. This is the same compound found in okra, and it is responsible for the pleasant coating quality of pumpkin leaf dishes.
sustainabilityTips: Using pumpkin leaves makes full use of the plant — nothing is wasted.
The pumpkin plant yields fruit, seeds (roasted as a snack), and leaves for cooking.

recipes.title: Kenyan Cabbage Fry
recipes.community: Enjoyed across all Kenyan communities — one of the most widely eaten vegetables
recipes.description: Kenyan Cabbage Fry — shredded cabbage stir-fried with onions, carrots, garlic, and a simple spice blend until tender-crisp and fragrant. One of the most widely eaten vegetables across Kenya — simple, affordable, and delicious alongside ugali or rice.
recipes.longDescription: Cabbage is one of the most democratic vegetables in Kenya — inexpensive, available everywhere, and capable of becoming something satisfying with just onions, garlic, and a little oil. The Kenyan way to cook cabbage is not to boil it but to fry it — high heat, quick cooking, tender-crisp. It is a staple in school canteens, home kitchens, and roadside eateries across the country.

substitutions.alternative: Chinese cabbage (napa) for a more tender result
Bell peppers for colour and sweetness

steps: Shred the cabbage finely and evenly for uniform cooking.
Heat oil in a large pan or wok over high heat.
Add onions and carrots. Stir-fry for 3—4 minutes until beginning to soften.
Add garlic. Cook 30 seconds.
Add the shredded cabbage. Toss and stir-fry for 4—5 minutes.
Add curry powder, paprika, salt, and pepper. Toss to coat.
Continue stir-frying for 2—3 minutes until the cabbage is tender-crisp — still with a slight bite.
Scatter with coriander and serve immediately.
chefTips: High heat and quick cooking preserves the cabbage's texture and natural sweetness.
Do not overcook — soggy cabbage is the most common mistake.
Add a splash of soy sauce for an extra depth of flavour.
commonMistakes: Overcooking — cabbage should still have a slight bite.
Low heat — causes the cabbage to steam and become watery rather than stir-fry.
recipes.storage: Best eaten fresh. Refrigerate for up to 2 days.
recipes.reheating: Reheat quickly in a hot pan.
healthBenefits: Rich in vitamin C and vitamin K.
Good source of folate and dietary fibre.
Very low in calories — just 85 kcal per serving.
Contains glucosinolates — compounds with anti-cancer properties.
recipes.culturalNote: Cabbage has become one of the most universally eaten vegetables in Kenya — present in school canteens, hospital meals, roadside food stalls, and family kitchens across every community. Its affordability and versatility make it an indispensable part of everyday Kenyan cooking.
regionalVariations: Classic Kenyan cabbage fry.
Spicy cabbage with extra chilli.
Cabbage with sausage.
Coconut cabbage — coastal style.
Cabbage and potato fry.

faqs.q: Can I add protein to this dish?
faqs.a: Yes — add beef, chicken, or sausage at the beginning before the vegetables. It becomes a complete one-pan meal.

recipes.cookingScience: High-heat stir-frying causes rapid water evaporation from the cabbage surface, concentrating the natural sugars and creating light caramelisation at the edges. Low heat causes the cabbage to release its moisture slowly, steaming it instead of frying — producing a soft, watery result.
sustainabilityTips: Cabbage is one of the most affordable and widely grown vegetables in Kenya.
The outer leaves, often discarded, are edible and nutritious.

recipes.title: Kenyan Spinach with Cream
recipes.community: Popular in urban Kenyan households and restaurants
recipes.description: Kenyan Spinach with Cream — fresh spinach wilted with garlic and onions then finished with cream or milk for a rich, silky, deeply satisfying vegetable dish. The Kenyan kitchen's most indulgent way with greens — simple, luxurious, and universally loved.
recipes.longDescription: Spinach with cream is one of those dishes that proves vegetables do not need to be ascetic to be good. A generous pour of cream transforms simple wilted spinach into something restaurant-worthy — silky, rich, and deeply satisfying. In Nairobi restaurants and at home celebrations, creamed spinach is the vegetable side that everyone quietly fights over.

substitutions.alternative: Full-fat milk, coconut cream, or natural yogurt
Olive oil for a lighter version
Managu or terere for a more traditional variation

steps: Wash the spinach thoroughly. Drain but do not dry completely — a little water helps it wilt.
Melt butter in a large pan over medium heat.
Cook onions until soft and translucent — 5 minutes.
Add garlic. Cook 30 seconds.
Add the spinach in batches — it wilts dramatically. Stir each batch until wilted before adding more.
Once all the spinach is wilted, cook for 2—3 minutes to release excess water.
Pour in the cream. Stir gently.
Season with salt, pepper, and nutmeg if using.
Simmer for 2—3 minutes until the cream is incorporated and slightly thickened.
Serve immediately.
chefTips: Do not overcook after adding cream — it should coat the spinach, not reduce to nothing.
Squeeze out excess water from the wilted spinach before adding cream — prevents a watery result.
A pinch of nutmeg is the classic partner to creamed spinach — do not skip it.
commonMistakes: Too much water in the spinach — the cream becomes diluted and watery.
Overcooking — the spinach loses its bright colour and the cream breaks.
recipes.storage: Best eaten fresh. Refrigerate for up to 2 days.
recipes.reheating: Warm gently over low heat.
healthBenefits: Iron and calcium from spinach.
Cream adds fat-soluble vitamins and makes the iron more absorbable.
Garlic provides antimicrobial allicin.
recipes.culturalNote: Creamed spinach occupies a special place in Kenyan restaurant menus — a touch of indulgence that elevates a simple vegetable into something celebratory. It appears at everything from hotel buffets to family Sunday lunches.
regionalVariations: Classic creamed spinach.
Coconut cream spinach — coastal style.
Spinach with cheese — popular in urban restaurants.
Spiced creamed spinach with nutmeg and garlic.

faqs.q: Can I make this vegan?
faqs.a: Yes — use olive oil instead of butter and coconut cream instead of dairy cream. The result is rich, fragrant, and equally satisfying.

recipes.cookingScience: Spinach contains approximately 92% water. When heated, this water is released — which is why spinach shrinks so dramatically. Squeezing out excess water before adding cream prevents dilution of the sauce and allows the cream to coat the leaves properly.
sustainabilityTips: Spinach grows quickly and can be harvested multiple times from the same plant.

recipes.title: Kenyan Mixed Traditional Greens
recipes.community: Prepared across all Kenyan communities
recipes.description: Kenyan Mixed Traditional Greens — mboga za kienyeji — a combination of managu, terere, kunde, or any available indigenous vegetables cooked together with onions, tomatoes, and garlic. The most nutritionally diverse vegetable dish in the Kenyan collection.
recipes.longDescription: Mboga za kienyeji — traditional vegetables — is less a fixed recipe than a philosophy: take what is available from the garden, combine it thoughtfully, and cook it simply. The mixture of different leafy greens creates a more complex flavour profile than any single green alone, and the nutritional combination is exceptional. This is ancestral Kenyan cooking at its most resourceful.
ingredients: Optional: ½ cup milk for creaminess

substitutions.alternative: Any available indigenous green or spinach

steps: Blanch the managu in boiling water for 2 minutes to reduce bitterness. Drain.
Heat oil over medium heat. Cook onions until soft — 5 minutes.
Add garlic. Cook 30 seconds.
Add tomatoes. Cook for 5—6 minutes until thick.
Add the managu first — it takes longest.
After 3 minutes, add terere. Stir to combine.
After another 2 minutes, add kunde. Add water.
Cover and cook for 5—8 minutes until all greens are tender.
Season, add coriander, and serve.
chefTips: Add greens in order of how long they take — tougher greens first, more tender ones last.
Each green contributes a different flavour note — the combination is more interesting than any single one.
A little peanut butter stirred in at the end adds richness and protein.
commonMistakes: Adding all greens at the same time — they cook at different rates.
Overcooking — mixed greens should retain some texture.
recipes.storage: Best eaten fresh. Refrigerate for up to 2 days.
recipes.reheating: Warm gently over low heat.
healthBenefits: Combining multiple greens maximises nutritional diversity.
Extraordinary combined iron, calcium, and vitamin content.
Very low in calories while being highly filling and nutritious.
recipes.culturalNote: Mboga za kienyeji represent the deep wisdom of traditional Kenyan agriculture — the practice of growing and eating multiple indigenous vegetable varieties together rather than relying on single crops. This biodiversity approach has sustained Kenyan communities for generations.
regionalVariations: Western Kenya mix — managu, terere, kunde.
Central Kenya mix — managu, pumpkin leaves.
Coastal mix — with coconut milk.
Any seasonal combination.

faqs.q: Can I use any combination of greens?
faqs.a: Yes — this recipe is designed to be flexible. Use whatever indigenous or garden greens are available. Sukuma wiki, pumpkin leaves, or spinach all work well.

recipes.cookingScience: Different leafy greens have different cell wall structures and cook at different rates. Managu, with its thicker leaves, takes 8—10 minutes; terere and kunde, with more delicate leaves, cook in 4—5 minutes. Staggered addition ensures all greens reach ideal tenderness simultaneously.
sustainabilityTips: Using multiple indigenous greens supports biodiversity in kitchen gardens.
Indigenous vegetables require fewer inputs than commercial varieties.

recipes.title: Kenyan Spider Plant Leaves
recipes.community: Luhya — primarily from Western Kenya
recipes.description: Sagaa — Kenyan Spider Plant Leaves — one of the most distinctive traditional vegetables of Western Kenya. The mildly aromatic, slightly musky leaves are sautéed with onions, tomatoes, and garlic into a uniquely flavoured vegetable dish beloved by the Luhya community.
recipes.longDescription: Sagaa has a flavour that is unmistakeable — slightly musky, herbal, and complex in a way that makes it unlike any other Kenyan vegetable. It is an acquired taste for some, but those who grow up eating it consider it one of the most flavourful and satisfying greens in the Kenyan repertoire. With ugali, it is a complete Western Kenya meal.
ingredients: 500g fresh sagaa leaves — washed and roughly chopped

substitutions.alternative: Bitter leaves or any mildly bitter green — note the flavour will be significantly different

steps: Wash sagaa leaves thoroughly. Remove any tough stems.
Blanch in boiling water for 3 minutes to reduce the bitterness and muskiness. Drain.
Heat oil over medium heat. Cook onions until soft — 5 minutes.
Add garlic. Cook 30 seconds.
Add tomatoes. Cook for 5—6 minutes until thick.
Add the blanched sagaa and water.
Cover and cook for 8—10 minutes until completely tender.
Season and serve with ugali.
chefTips: Blanching is essential for sagaa — it reduces the strong musky aroma to a pleasant aromatic quality.
Longer cooking suits sagaa — it mellows and develops in flavour over 10 minutes.
Milk or cream stirred in at the end balances the musky flavour beautifully.
commonMistakes: Skipping the blanching — produces a very strongly flavoured dish that can overwhelm.
Undercooking — sagaa benefits from a longer cook than more delicate greens.

heritage.origin: Western Kenya — Luhya community, traditionally grown in homestead gardens
heritage.history: Sagaa (Cleome gynandra, commonly known as spider plant) is one of the oldest cultivated leafy vegetables in Africa. In the Luhya community of Western Kenya, it has been a homestead garden staple for generations, prized for its distinctive musky aroma and its remarkable ability to grow vigorously in poor soils.
heritage.modernEvolution: Once primarily a rural Western Kenya vegetable, sagaa is gaining appreciation among health-conscious urban Kenyans for its exceptional nutritional density.

recipes.storage: Best eaten fresh. Refrigerate for up to 2 days.
recipes.reheating: Warm gently over low heat.
healthBenefits: Rich in calcium, iron, and vitamins A and C.
Contains glucosinolates with potential anti-cancer properties.
Very low in calories.
recipes.culturalNote: Sagaa is a defining vegetable of Luhya food culture in Western Kenya — deeply associated with homestead garden traditions and the resourceful agricultural practices of the community.
regionalVariations: Classic sagaa with tomatoes.
Sagaa with milk — creamier version.
Mixed sagaa and managu.

faqs.q: What does sagaa taste like?
faqs.a: Sagaa has a distinctive musky, slightly aromatic flavour with gentle bitterness — unlike any other Kenyan vegetable. It is strong enough to be memorable but mellows significantly with blanching and cooking.

faqs.q: Where can I find sagaa?
faqs.a: In Kenya, sagaa is found in Western Kenya markets and increasingly in Nairobi markets. Outside Kenya, it may be available in African grocery stores as cleome or spider plant.

recipes.cookingScience: The distinctive aroma of sagaa comes from glucosinolates and other sulphur-containing compounds. Blanching breaks down some of these compounds and releases others into the water, significantly moderating the intensity while retaining the pleasant aromatic character.
sustainabilityTips: Sagaa is one of the most drought-resistant traditional vegetables — grows in poor soils with minimal water.
Highly recommended for kitchen gardens in Western Kenya.

recipes.title: Kenyan Ethiopian Kale
recipes.community: Popular in urban Kenyan kitchens — increasingly grown across Kenya
recipes.description: Kenyan Ethiopian Kale — lacinato kale (also called Ethiopian kale or dinosaur kale) prepared the Kenyan way with onions, tomatoes, garlic, and a simple spice blend. Tender, slightly nutty, and more flavourful than regular sukuma wiki.
recipes.longDescription: Ethiopian kale (Brassica carinata) is a robustly flavoured variety of kale that grows very well in East African conditions and has become increasingly popular in Kenyan urban gardens and markets. Its darker, more intensely flavoured leaves have a slight nuttiness that regular sukuma wiki lacks, and it responds beautifully to the classic Kenyan preparation of onions, tomatoes, and garlic.
ingredients: 500g Ethiopian kale (lacinato kale) — stems removed, leaves roughly chopped

substitutions.alternative: Regular sukuma wiki (collard greens) or curly kale

steps: Remove the tough central stems from the kale leaves. Roughly chop the leaves.
Heat oil over medium heat. Cook onions until golden — 6 minutes.
Add garlic (and ginger if using). Cook 30 seconds.
Add tomatoes and curry powder if using. Cook for 5—6 minutes until thick.
Add the kale and water.
Stir to coat with the sauce. Cover and cook for 6—8 minutes until the kale is tender.
Season with salt and pepper. Serve immediately.
chefTips: Ethiopian kale holds its texture better than regular sukuma wiki — it benefits from slightly longer cooking.
Massaging the raw leaves with a little salt before cooking breaks down the cell walls and reduces bitterness.
Adding lemon juice just before serving brightens the earthy flavour.
commonMistakes: Undercooking — Ethiopian kale needs 6—8 minutes minimum to become tender.
Not removing the tough stems — they take much longer to cook than the leaves.
recipes.storage: Best eaten fresh. Refrigerate for up to 2 days.
recipes.reheating: Warm gently over low heat.
healthBenefits: One of the most nutrient-dense vegetables — exceptional levels of vitamins K, C, and A.
Rich in calcium and iron.
High in antioxidants including lutein and zeaxanthin for eye health.
recipes.culturalNote: Ethiopian kale represents the expanding diversity of traditional Kenyan vegetable cultivation — a robust, highly nutritious variety that is perfectly suited to the Kenyan climate and is increasingly finding its place in Kenyan kitchens alongside sukuma wiki.
regionalVariations: Classic Kenyan preparation with tomatoes.
Ethiopian kale with coconut milk.
Spiced Ethiopian kale with cumin.

faqs.q: What is the difference between Ethiopian kale and sukuma wiki?
faqs.a: Both are in the Brassica family but different species. Ethiopian kale (Brassica carinata) has darker, more robust leaves with a more intense, nutty flavour. Sukuma wiki (Brassica oleracea) is milder and more widely grown in Kenya.

recipes.cookingScience: Kale contains tough cell walls reinforced with cellulose. Cooking breaks down these walls progressively — adequate cooking time (6—8 minutes minimum) is needed to achieve a tender result. The glucosinolates that give kale its slight bitterness also partially break down during cooking.
sustainabilityTips: Ethiopian kale is extremely well-adapted to East African growing conditions — drought-tolerant and pest-resistant.
Can be harvested leaf by leaf, allowing the plant to continue producing.

recipes.title: Kenyan Okra Stew
recipes.community: Swahili and Kamba — popular along the coast and in Eastern Kenya
recipes.description: Kenyan Okra Stew — fresh okra sautéed with onions, tomatoes, garlic, and Swahili coastal spices until tender and naturally silky. A beloved traditional vegetable dish along Kenya's coast and in Eastern Kenya.
recipes.longDescription: Okra (bamia) is particularly beloved in Kenyan coastal cooking, where its natural mucilage is valued rather than avoided — it creates the silky, coating quality of the sauce that makes this stew so satisfying. With fresh tomatoes and Swahili spices, bamia stew is one of the most comforting and distinctive vegetable dishes in Kenya.
ingredients: 400g fresh okra — tips and tops trimmed, sliced

substitutions.alternative: Frozen okra — thaw and dry before using

steps: Wash okra and dry completely — moisture increases sliminess.
Trim the tops and tips. Slice into 2cm rounds.
Heat oil over high heat. Add okra and fry for 3—4 minutes until lightly browned — this reduces sliminess.
Remove okra and set aside.
In the same pan, cook onions until golden — 6 minutes.
Add garlic and ginger. Cook 30 seconds.
Add tomatoes, curry powder, and turmeric. Cook for 6—8 minutes until thick.
Return okra to the pan. Stir gently.
Simmer for 5—8 minutes until okra is tender.
Scatter coriander and serve.
chefTips: Frying the okra first is the key step — it significantly reduces the sliminess that puts many people off okra.
Completely dry okra before cooking — moisture activates the mucilage.
A splash of lemon juice or vinegar during cooking also helps reduce sliminess.
commonMistakes: Not drying the okra — produces a very slimy result.
Skipping the initial frying — the okra remains slimy throughout.
Overcooking — okra becomes mushy.
recipes.storage: Best eaten fresh. Refrigerate for up to 2 days.
recipes.reheating: Warm gently over low heat.
healthBenefits: Rich in soluble fibre that supports healthy cholesterol levels.
Good source of vitamins C and K.
Mucilage in okra supports gut health and digestion.
Very low in calories.
recipes.culturalNote: Bamia stew is particularly beloved in Swahili coastal cooking, where it has been prepared for generations. Along the coast, okra's natural mucilage is embraced rather than avoided — seen as a quality that makes the stew nourishing and satisfying.
regionalVariations: Classic Swahili bamia stew.
Coconut okra — coastal style.
Okra with shrimp.
Spicy okra stew.
Okra with tomatoes only — the simplest version.

faqs.q: How do I reduce okra's sliminess?
faqs.a: Three techniques work: fry the okra in a hot pan before adding to the stew; dry the okra completely before cooking; add a splash of lemon juice or vinegar to the dish during cooking. Using all three gives the least slimy result.

recipes.cookingScience: Okra's sliminess comes from mucilage — a complex mixture of polysaccharides. High-heat frying denatures the proteins that bind the mucilage network, reducing its ability to create the characteristic slimy texture. Acid (lemon juice or vinegar) also breaks down the mucilage network.
sustainabilityTips: Okra grows prolifically in Kenyan conditions with minimal water.
The entire plant is useful — seeds can be roasted, pods eaten, and leaves used as a vegetable.

recipes.title: Kenyan Eggplant Stew
recipes.community: Swahili — popular along the Kenyan coast
recipes.description: Kenyan Eggplant Stew — cubed aubergine cooked with onions, tomatoes, garlic, ginger, and coastal spices until tender and rich. A beloved Swahili coastal preparation that transforms eggplant into something deeply flavourful.
recipes.longDescription: Eggplant (biringanya) arrived on the Kenyan coast through centuries of Indian Ocean trade and has become deeply embedded in Swahili coastal cooking. The vegetable absorbs surrounding flavours beautifully — cooked with a fragrant tomato base and Swahili spices, it develops a rich, meaty quality that makes it one of the most satisfying vegetarian dishes in the coastal repertoire.
steps: Salt the cubed eggplant, toss to coat, and leave for 15 minutes. This draws out bitterness and excess moisture. Rinse and pat dry.
Heat oil in a large pan over medium-high heat. Fry eggplant cubes for 4—5 minutes until lightly browned on the outside. Remove and set aside.
In the same pan, cook onions until golden — 6 minutes.
Add garlic and ginger. Cook 30 seconds.
Add tomatoes, curry powder, turmeric, and paprika. Cook for 6—8 minutes until thick.
Return the browned eggplant. Stir gently.
Cover and simmer for 8—10 minutes until completely tender.
Add lemon juice and coriander. Serve.
chefTips: Salting the eggplant first is important — it removes bitterness and prevents the eggplant from absorbing excess oil during frying.
Brown the eggplant before adding to the sauce — it develops a richer flavour and holds its shape better.
Eggplant absorbs flavour beautifully — do not rush the final simmer.
commonMistakes: Not salting first — the dish can be bitter.
Skipping the browning step — eggplant becomes mushy in the sauce.
Too much oil — eggplant absorbs oil very readily.
recipes.storage: Refrigerate for up to 3 days.
recipes.reheating: Warm gently over medium-low heat.
healthBenefits: Rich in antioxidants including nasunin in the purple skin.
Good source of dietary fibre.
Very low in calories.
Contains chlorogenic acid with anti-inflammatory properties.
recipes.culturalNote: Biringanya stew is a beloved preparation along Kenya's Swahili coast, reflecting the centuries of Indian Ocean trade that introduced eggplant and the spices that bring it to life in this dish.
regionalVariations: Classic Swahili eggplant stew.
Coconut eggplant — with coconut milk.
Spicy eggplant stew.
Eggplant with potatoes.

faqs.q: Is eggplant traditional in Kenyan cooking?
faqs.a: Eggplant is particularly traditional in Swahili coastal cooking, where it arrived through Indian Ocean trade centuries ago. It is less common in inland Kenyan cooking but increasingly popular in urban markets.

recipes.cookingScience: Eggplant has a highly porous flesh that absorbs oil rapidly. Salting first draws out moisture through osmosis and slightly collapses the cell structure, reducing the amount of oil absorbed during frying — this is why salting is worth the 15-minute wait.
sustainabilityTips: Eggplant grows well in Kenyan coastal conditions with moderate water.

recipes.title: Kenyan Vegetable Medley
recipes.community: Popular across all Kenyan communities — especially urban households
recipes.description: Kenyan Vegetable Medley — a colourful stir-fry of cabbage, carrots, green beans, capsicum, onions, and tomatoes cooked with garlic and a simple Kenyan spice blend. The most versatile, nutritionally diverse, and universally appealing vegetable side dish in the Kenyan repertoire.
recipes.longDescription: Vegetable medley is the contemporary Kenyan kitchen at its most resourceful — a colourful, quick stir-fry of whatever vegetables are available, elevated by garlic, a good spice blend, and high heat. It is the side dish that goes with everything, accommodates any dietary need, and transforms humble ingredients into something bright and satisfying.
steps: Prepare all vegetables before starting — stir-frying moves quickly.
Heat oil in a large wok or pan over high heat.
Add onions and carrots. Stir-fry for 2—3 minutes.
Add green beans. Stir-fry for 2 minutes.
Add garlic. Cook 30 seconds.
Add bell peppers and cabbage. Toss and stir-fry for 2—3 minutes.
Add tomatoes, curry powder, paprika, salt, and pepper.
Stir-fry for 2—3 minutes more — vegetables should be tender-crisp, not soft.
Add soy sauce if using. Toss.
Scatter coriander and serve immediately.
chefTips: Prepare (mise en place) everything before turning on the heat — stir-frying happens fast.
Add vegetables in order of density: carrots and beans first, soft vegetables last.
High heat is essential — low heat steams the vegetables rather than stir-frying them.
Do not overcrowd the pan — cook in two batches if needed.
commonMistakes: Low heat — produces steamed, soggy vegetables rather than bright, crisp stir-fry.
Adding everything at once — different vegetables need different cooking times.
Overcooking — vegetables should retain colour and a slight crunch.
recipes.storage: Best eaten immediately. Refrigerate for up to 2 days.
recipes.reheating: Reheat quickly in a hot pan to preserve texture.
healthBenefits: Extraordinary vitamin and mineral diversity from multiple vegetables.
Rich in vitamins A, C, and K from the variety of greens.
High in dietary fibre from multiple sources.
Very low in calories while being highly filling.
recipes.culturalNote: Vegetable medley has become a staple of Kenyan urban cooking — practical, adaptable, and nutritious. It represents the contemporary Kenyan kitchen embracing both traditional and modern ingredients in one versatile, colourful dish.
regionalVariations: Classic Kenyan vegetable medley.
Spicy medley with extra chilli.
Coconut vegetable medley — coastal style.
Asian-Kenyan fusion with soy sauce and sesame.

faqs.q: What vegetables can I add?
faqs.a: Almost any vegetable works — broccoli, courgette, mange tout, baby corn, mushrooms, or spinach all integrate well. Add denser vegetables first, delicate ones last.

faqs.q: Can I add protein?
faqs.a: Yes — chicken, beef, tofu, or shrimp can be stir-fried first and set aside, then returned to the pan with the vegetables. This becomes a complete one-pan meal.

recipes.cookingScience: Stir-frying in a hot pan creates the Maillard reaction on the surfaces of vegetables while the brief cooking time preserves vitamins and minerals that are lost with longer cooking methods. The high heat also drives off moisture quickly, preventing steaming and maintaining texture.
sustainabilityTips: Vegetable medley is the perfect use for miscellaneous vegetables before they spoil — reducing food waste significantly.
Buying seasonal local vegetables minimises transport emissions.

recipes.title: Kenyan Omelette
recipes.community: Enjoyed across all Kenyan communities
recipes.description: The Kenyan Omelette is a robust, flavour-packed breakfast staple — eggs beaten and filled with onions, tomatoes, capsicum, fresh coriander, and chilli, then folded into a golden, satisfying meal. More substantial than a French omelette and entirely its own thing.
recipes.longDescription: The Kenyan omelette is not delicate. It is generous — loaded with onions, tomatoes, peppers, and coriander, cooked through rather than set soft, and eaten with bread or chapati for a breakfast that sustains you all morning. At every Kenyan roadside kiosk, hotel buffet, and family kitchen, the omelette is a morning constant.
steps: Beat the eggs with milk, salt, and pepper until well combined and slightly frothy.
Stir in the onion, tomato, bell pepper, chilli, and coriander.
Heat oil or butter in a non-stick pan over medium heat.
Pour in the egg mixture. Allow to set on the bottom for 1—2 minutes without stirring.
As the edges set, gently lift and tilt the pan to allow uncooked egg to flow underneath.
When the top is just set but still slightly glossy, fold in half.
Cook for 1 more minute until golden on the outside and cooked through.
Slide onto a plate and serve immediately with bread, chapati, or ugali.
chefTips: Medium heat is the key — too high burns the outside before the inside sets.
The Kenyan omelette is cooked through, not soft and runny like a French omelette — this is correct.
Finely dicing all the vegetables ensures they cook through in the brief cooking time.
A well-seasoned non-stick pan makes the difference between a perfect omelette and a stuck mess.
commonMistakes: Too high heat — burnt outside, raw inside.
Too much filling — the omelette does not set properly.
Not beating the eggs enough — produces a flat, dense result.
recipes.storage: Best eaten immediately.
recipes.reheating: Not recommended — omelettes are best fresh.
healthBenefits: Complete protein from eggs — all essential amino acids.
Rich in B12, vitamin D, and choline for brain health.
High in selenium and iodine.
Vegetables add vitamins A and C.
recipes.culturalNote: The Kenyan omelette is a breakfast institution — present in every hotel, guesthouse, and roadside kiosk across the country. Its generous filling of vegetables and spices makes it distinctly Kenyan — robust, satisfying, and full of character.
regionalVariations: Classic Kenyan omelette with tomatoes and onions.
Coastal omelette — with coconut milk in the eggs.
Cheese omelette — popular in Nairobi restaurants.
Spicy omelette with extra chilli.
Sausage omelette.

faqs.q: Can I add cheese?
faqs.a: Absolutely — grated cheddar or mozzarella added just before folding melts beautifully and adds richness. This is a popular variation in Kenyan urban restaurants.

faqs.q: Can I add meat?
faqs.a: Yes — diced sausage, minced beef, or leftover chicken added to the filling makes this a more substantial meal.

recipes.cookingScience: Eggs contain proteins (primarily ovalbumin and ovotransferrin) that denature and coagulate when heated. The milk added to the beaten eggs dilutes the protein concentration slightly, producing a more tender, less rubbery omelette. Beating introduces air, which expands during cooking and creates a lighter texture.
sustainabilityTips: Eggs are one of the most nutrient-efficient protein sources with a lower environmental footprint than meat.
Buy from local Kenyan free-range farms where possible.

recipes.title: Kenyan Egg Curry
recipes.community: Popular across Kenya — strong Indian-Kenyan culinary influence
recipes.description: Kenyan Egg Curry — hard-boiled eggs simmered in a richly spiced tomato and onion curry sauce with garlic, ginger, and garam masala. One of Kenya's most satisfying budget-friendly meals — the combination of creamy eggs and bold curry sauce is extraordinary.
recipes.longDescription: Egg curry is one of those dishes that seems simple until you eat it — and then you understand why it is beloved across the Indian-Kenyan culinary tradition and has become a staple in Kenyan homes. Hard-boiled eggs, halved or scored and simmered in a deeply spiced tomato sauce, absorb the curry beautifully. The result is rich, warming, and deeply satisfying at a fraction of the cost of meat curries.
steps: Hard-boil the eggs: place in cold water, bring to a boil, cook for 10 minutes. Transfer to cold water immediately, then peel.
Score the peeled eggs 3—4 times with a knife — this allows the curry sauce to penetrate and flavour the eggs.
Optional: shallow-fry the peeled eggs in a little oil for 2—3 minutes until lightly golden all over. This adds a pleasant texture.
Heat oil in a pan. Cook onions until deeply golden — 10 minutes.
Add garlic and ginger. Cook 1 minute.
Add tomatoes and tomato paste. Cook for 8 minutes until thick.
Add all spices except garam masala. Stir 1 minute.
Add water. Bring to a gentle simmer.
Add eggs halved or whole. Spoon sauce over them gently.
Simmer for 8—10 minutes until the eggs have absorbed some of the curry flavour.
Stir in garam masala. Scatter coriander and serve.
chefTips: Scoring the eggs is the most important step — it allows the curry sauce to penetrate the white, infusing every bite.
Shallow-frying the eggs before adding them to the curry creates a lightly crispy exterior that absorbs sauce differently — the texture contrast is excellent.
Do not rush the onion and tomato base — the deeper it cooks, the richer the curry.
commonMistakes: Not scoring the eggs — they stay plain white while the sauce stays on the outside.
Under-cooking the base — a pale, thin sauce produces a flat curry.
Overcooking in the curry — the eggs become rubbery.
recipes.storage: Refrigerate for up to 3 days.
recipes.reheating: Reheat gently on stovetop over low heat.
healthBenefits: Complete protein from eggs — highly bioavailable.
Turmeric provides curcumin.
Very affordable nutrition.
Eggs provide choline — essential for brain health.
recipes.culturalNote: Egg curry reflects the deep Indian-Kenyan culinary heritage — one of the most beloved budget-friendly meals that delivers all the satisfaction of a meat curry at a fraction of the cost. It is a staple in Kenyan homes and restaurants nationwide.
regionalVariations: Classic Kenyan egg curry.
Coconut egg curry — coastal style.
Dry egg curry — sauce reduced to a coating.
Spicy egg curry.

faqs.q: Can I use soft-boiled eggs?
faqs.a: Yes — soft-boiled eggs (6 minutes) create a runnier yolk that mixes beautifully into the curry sauce. They are more delicate to handle but the result is extraordinary.

recipes.cookingScience: Scoring the egg white creates channels through which the curry sauce can diffuse via osmosis during simmering. The hot sauce gradually displaces some of the water in the egg white, carrying flavour compounds with it — this is why scored eggs taste so much better than unscored ones in curry.
sustainabilityTips: Egg curry is one of the most affordable and environmentally friendly protein-rich meals.

recipes.title: Kenyan Egg Stew
recipes.community: Enjoyed across all Kenyan communities — a beloved quick meal
recipes.description: Kenyan Egg Stew — eggs poached directly in a fragrant tomato, onion, and garlic sauce until perfectly set. Quick, nourishing, affordable, and deeply satisfying — one of Kenya's most beloved everyday meals. Ready in 30 minutes and loved by the whole family.
recipes.longDescription: Egg stew is the Kenyan kitchen at its most resourceful and most satisfying. A rich tomato sauce is built in minutes, then eggs are cracked directly into the sauce and poached until the whites are set and the yolks are still slightly runny. The yolk breaks into the sauce as you eat, enriching it further. Scooped with ugali or chapati, it is one of the most complete and comforting meals in the Kenyan repertoire.
steps: Heat oil in a large wide pan over medium heat.
Cook onions until soft and golden — 8 minutes.
Add garlic and ginger. Cook 1 minute.
Add tomatoes and tomato paste. Cook for 8—10 minutes until a thick sauce forms.
Add curry powder and paprika. Stir 30 seconds.
Add water and bring to a gentle simmer.
Make 6 small wells in the sauce. Crack one egg into each well.
Cover and cook for 5—8 minutes until the egg whites are set but yolks are still slightly runny.
Season. Scatter with coriander.
Serve immediately — directly from the pan.
chefTips: The sauce should be thick before you add the eggs — a thin sauce produces uneven poaching.
Do not stir after adding the eggs — let them poach undisturbed.
A wide pan allows more eggs to cook evenly without crowding.
Cover while the eggs cook — the trapped steam sets the tops of the whites without flipping.
commonMistakes: Thin sauce — eggs spread too much and cook unevenly.
Stirring after adding eggs — breaks the yolks prematurely.
Overcooking — the yolks become hard and the dish loses its characteristic richness.
recipes.storage: Best eaten immediately — eggs change texture when refrigerated in sauce.
recipes.reheating: Not recommended — the eggs overcook when reheated.
healthBenefits: Excellent complete protein from eggs.
Tomatoes provide lycopene and vitamin C.
Very affordable and highly nourishing.
recipes.culturalNote: Egg stew is one of the most universally beloved meals in Kenya — quick, affordable, and satisfying at any time of day. From breakfast in a Nairobi apartment to lunch in a Western Kenya homestead, mayai ya mchuzi is a constant across the country.
regionalVariations: Classic Kenyan egg stew.
Spicy egg stew with extra chilli.
Coconut egg stew — coastal style.
Egg stew with potatoes.
Egg stew with spinach.

faqs.q: Can I use hard-boiled eggs instead?
faqs.a: Yes — see KEN092 (Egg Curry) which uses pre-boiled eggs in a similar sauce. The poaching method here is faster and produces a more integrated, saucier result.

faqs.q: How do I know when the eggs are done?
faqs.a: The white should be completely set and opaque — press gently with the back of a spoon to check. The yolk should have a slight jiggle for a runny result. Cover for the final 2 minutes for firmer yolks.

recipes.cookingScience: Poaching eggs in tomato sauce is essentially the same as poaching in water — the proteins in the egg white denature and coagulate as they heat. Tomato sauce conducts heat efficiently and adds flavour compounds that infuse the white as it sets. The acidity of the tomatoes also helps the egg white coagulate more quickly.
sustainabilityTips: One of the most affordable and lowest-impact protein meals available.

recipes.title: Kenyan Spanish Omelette
recipes.community: Popular in urban Kenyan households and restaurants
recipes.description: Kenyan Spanish Omelette — a thick, hearty frittata of eggs, potatoes, onions, tomatoes, and capsicum cooked slowly until set through. The Kenyan adaptation adds local spices and coriander to the classic Spanish tortilla concept — more substantial and deeply flavoured.
recipes.longDescription: The Kenyan spin on a Spanish omelette keeps the essence — thick egg and potato cake — but adds the characteristic Kenyan flavour profile: tomatoes, coriander, paprika, and curry powder. The result is something between a frittata and a Kenyan omelette, sliceable like a pie and satisfying enough to be a complete meal. It is ideal for meal prep — it keeps well and tastes even better the next day.
ingredients: 2 medium potatoes — peeled, thinly sliced and par-cooked
equipment: Oven-safe frying pan or non-stick pan
steps: Par-cook the potato slices: boil for 5—7 minutes until just tender but still holding shape. Drain and cool.
Heat 2 tbsp oil in a pan over medium heat. Cook onions for 5 minutes until soft.
Add tomatoes and bell pepper. Cook for 3 minutes.
Beat eggs with milk, paprika, curry powder, salt, and pepper. Stir in coriander.
Add par-cooked potato slices to the pan with the onion and tomato mixture.
Pour the beaten egg mixture over everything. Shake the pan gently to distribute evenly.
Cook over low heat for 8—10 minutes until the edges and bottom are set but the top is still slightly liquid.
Finish option 1 (grill): place the pan under a grill for 3—4 minutes until the top is set and golden.
Finish option 2 (flip): place a plate over the pan and flip the omelette onto it, then slide back into the pan to cook the other side for 3—4 minutes.
Cut into wedges and serve.
chefTips: Par-cooking the potatoes first ensures they cook through in the brief egg-cooking time.
Very low heat is essential — this must cook slowly to set through without burning.
The omelette is ready on the bottom when a spatula slid underneath meets no resistance.
commonMistakes: Raw potatoes — they will not cook through in the egg-cooking time.
Too high heat — burns the bottom before the top sets.
Rushing — this omelette takes 10 minutes minimum on low heat.
recipes.storage: Refrigerate for up to 2 days. Eat cold or reheat briefly.
recipes.reheating: Microwave briefly or warm in a pan over low heat.
healthBenefits: Complete protein from eggs.
Potatoes provide complex carbohydrates.
A balanced, filling meal.
recipes.culturalNote: The Kenyan Spanish omelette has become popular in urban kitchens as a meal-prep-friendly, budget-conscious option that is equally good for breakfast, lunch, or a light dinner.
regionalVariations: Classic Kenyan Spanish omelette.
Spicy version with chilli.
Cheese and tomato version.
Sausage and potato version.

faqs.q: Can I add cheese?
faqs.a: Yes — grated cheddar scattered over the top just before grilling melts beautifully and adds richness.

faqs.q: Can I make this ahead?
faqs.a: Yes — Spanish omelette keeps well for 2 days refrigerated and can be eaten cold, at room temperature, or reheated briefly.

recipes.cookingScience: The thick egg and potato cake is set by gentle, prolonged heat — the proteins need time to coagulate throughout the mass without the exterior burning. This is why a Spanish omelette is cooked on very low heat for a longer time than a regular omelette.
sustainabilityTips: A great use for leftover cooked potatoes — reduces food waste.

recipes.title: Kenyan Boiled Egg Curry
recipes.community: Swahili — popular nationwide with coastal spice influence
recipes.description: Kenyan Boiled Egg Curry with Swahili coastal spices — hard-boiled eggs fried until golden then simmered in a richly spiced coconut-tomato sauce with cardamom, cinnamon, and fresh coriander. The coastal elevation of the everyday egg curry — fragrant, rich, and deeply satisfying.
recipes.longDescription: This is egg curry elevated with the full Swahili coastal spice palette — whole cardamom, cinnamon, and cloves adding aromatic depth to the tomato base, finished with a generous pour of coconut milk that transforms it into something truly special. The eggs, fried first until golden, develop a slightly crispy exterior that absorbs the coconut sauce beautifully during simmering.
steps: Heat 2 tbsp oil in a pan over medium-high heat. Add the peeled hard-boiled eggs and fry for 3—4 minutes, turning, until golden brown all over. Remove and set aside.
In the same pan, add remaining oil. Add whole spices (cardamom, cinnamon, cloves) and fry 30 seconds.
Add onions. Cook until deeply golden — 10 minutes.
Add garlic and ginger. Cook 1 minute.
Add tomatoes, curry powder, turmeric, and paprika. Cook for 8—10 minutes until thick.
Pour in coconut milk. Stir gently. Bring to a gentle simmer — do not boil hard.
Add the fried eggs. Spoon sauce over them.
Simmer for 8—10 minutes.
Stir in garam masala and lemon juice.
Scatter coriander and serve with rice.
chefTips: Frying the eggs first creates a golden, lightly crispy exterior that absorbs the coconut curry sauce much better than unfried eggs.
The whole spices (cardamom, cinnamon, cloves) at the beginning build the aromatic base of this coastal curry — do not skip them.
Never boil the coconut milk vigorously — it splits.
commonMistakes: Boiling the coconut milk hard — it separates and becomes oily.
Skipping the initial egg frying — the eggs remain smooth and do not absorb the sauce as deeply.
recipes.storage: Refrigerate for up to 3 days.
recipes.reheating: Reheat very gently on stovetop over low heat.
healthBenefits: Complete protein from eggs.
Coconut milk adds healthy MCTs.
Aromatic spices contribute antioxidant compounds.
recipes.culturalNote: This coastal egg curry reflects the Swahili tradition of elevating simple everyday ingredients with aromatic spices and coconut milk — a culinary philosophy that has shaped the most celebrated dishes of the Kenyan coast for centuries.
regionalVariations: Classic coastal coconut egg curry.
Dry version — coconut milk reduced to a glaze.
Extra spicy with chilli.
With potatoes added.

faqs.q: Is this different from KEN092 (Egg Curry)?
faqs.a: Yes — this coastal version adds whole Swahili spices (cardamom, cinnamon, cloves) for a more aromatic base, and finishes with coconut milk for a richer, creamier sauce. KEN092 is the classic everyday version; this is the celebratory coastal version.

recipes.cookingScience: Frying the egg creates micro-fissures and a porous texture on the white's surface through protein contraction and slight dehydration. This porous exterior absorbs the surrounding sauce by capillary action during simmering — creating a far more flavourful egg than one that was simply boiled and added to sauce.
sustainabilityTips: This dish demonstrates how coconut milk can transform affordable eggs into a special meal — sustainability and indulgence together.

recipes.title: Kenyan Mombasa Pilau
recipes.community: Swahili — Mombasa tradition
recipes.description: Pilau ya Mombasa is Kenya's most celebrated rice dish — a feast-worthy one-pot of basmati rice and meat cooked with deeply caramelised onions, whole coastal spices, and rich stock until each grain is dark, fragrant, and deeply flavoured. The definitive Kenyan pilau.
recipes.longDescription: What distinguishes Mombasa pilau from all other versions is the onions. They must be cooked for a full 20—25 minutes until they are almost black — not burnt, but deeply caramelised into something sweet, rich, and intensely flavoured. This dark onion base is the soul of authentic Mombasa pilau and the reason it is unlike any other rice dish in the world.
ingredients: 3 cups (600g) basmati rice — rinsed and soaked 30 minutes

substitutions.alternative: Chicken — reduce meat simmering time to 25 minutes
Vegetable oil — authentic but slightly less rich

equipment: Large heavy-bottomed pot with tight lid
steps: Heat ghee or oil in a very large pot over medium heat. Add the sliced onions.
Cook the onions, stirring every 5 minutes, for 20—25 minutes until deeply, almost blackly caramelised. This is the defining step — do not rush it.
Add whole spices (cardamom, cinnamon, cloves, cumin, peppercorns). Fry 1 minute.
Add garlic and ginger. Cook 1 minute.
Add tomatoes and turmeric. Cook for 10 minutes until very thick and dark.
Add the meat. Brown for 5—6 minutes, stirring.
Add 3 cups of stock. Cover and simmer for 45—60 minutes until the meat is completely tender.
Add the soaked, drained rice and remaining 3 cups stock. Stir once gently.
Bring to a boil, then reduce to the absolute lowest heat. Cover tightly.
Cook undisturbed for 20 minutes until all liquid is absorbed.
Rest covered for 10 minutes. Fluff gently and garnish with coriander and fried onions.
chefTips: The 20—25 minute onion caramelisation is non-negotiable — it is the entire foundation of Mombasa pilau. Pale onions produce pale, flavourless pilau.
The stock must be deeply flavoured — use homemade or a good quality stock.
The pot must be heavy — thin pots create hot spots and burn the bottom rice.
Do not lift the lid during the rice cooking phase.
commonMistakes: Under-caramelising the onions — the most common mistake. 20 minutes minimum.
Too much liquid — makes the rice mushy.
Thin pot — burns the bottom before the top is cooked.

regionalMap.primaryRegion: Mombasa — the spiritual home of Kenyan pilau
regionalMap.alsoCommonIn: Nationwide at celebrations — the most iconic version of the dish

heritage.origin: Mombasa, Kenyan Swahili Coast — centuries of Arab, Persian, and Indian Ocean culinary influence
heritage.history: Mombasa pilau is considered the original and most authentic version of Kenyan pilau. Brought to the Swahili coast through Indian Ocean trade routes, it has been refined over centuries in the Old Town kitchens of Mombasa into the deeply aromatic, caramelised-onion-forward dish that defines Kenyan celebration cooking. Every wedding, Eid feast, and important gathering along the coast centres around a large pot of Mombasa pilau.
heritage.modernEvolution: While traditionally cooked over charcoal in large community pots for weddings feeding hundreds, modern Mombasa pilau is made on gas stoves in home kitchens. The technique — especially the deep caramelisation of onions — remains unchanged.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate for up to 3 days. Freeze for up to 2 months.
recipes.reheating: Sprinkle with water and reheat gently in a covered pot or microwave.
healthBenefits: Complete meal — protein, carbohydrates, and aromatic spice benefits.
Whole spices contribute antioxidant compounds.
One-pot cooking preserves more nutrients than multi-stage preparations.
recipes.culturalNote: Mombasa pilau is Kenya's most celebrated rice dish and one of the defining expressions of Swahili culinary culture. At every important occasion — Eid, weddings, funerals, homecomings — the aroma of pilau cooking is the signal that something significant is being marked. It is the food of memory, community, and shared celebration.
regionalVariations: Mombasa beef pilau — the most traditional.
Mombasa goat pilau — equally authentic.
Lamu-style pilau — with rose water and extra spice.
Nairobi-style pilau — lighter spice, more accessible.

faqs.q: Why is Mombasa pilau different from other pilau?
faqs.a: The depth of onion caramelisation, the use of ghee, and the quality of the whole spice blend distinguish Mombasa pilau. The onions are cooked until almost black — a step that requires patience but produces an incomparable depth of flavour.

faqs.q: Can I make this vegetarian?
faqs.a: Yes — see KEN098 (Vegetable Pilau). Omit the meat and use vegetable stock. The deeply caramelised onion technique remains the same.

recipes.cookingScience: The extended caramelisation of onions converts fructose and glucose through the Maillard reaction and caramelisation simultaneously, producing hundreds of new flavour compounds — including furaneol, pyrazines, and caramel compounds — that cannot be achieved by shorter cooking. This is why 20 minutes of caramelisation tastes so dramatically different from 5 minutes.
sustainabilityTips: Cook a large batch — pilau feeds many from one efficient cooking session.
The pilau pot at the base often develops a prized crust (similar to Persian tahdig) — serve this too.

recipes.title: Kenyan Swahili Biryani
recipes.community: Swahili — the pinnacle of coastal celebration cooking
recipes.description: Kenyan Swahili Biryani — the most elaborate and celebrated dish in Swahili cuisine. Spiced beef or goat layered with par-cooked saffron rice, deeply caramelised onions, fresh herbs, and aromatic whole spices, then sealed and slow-steamed (dum) until each grain carries the full depth of coastal flavour. Reserved for the most important occasions.
recipes.longDescription: Swahili biryani is not an everyday dish — it is the pinnacle of Kenyan coastal cooking, prepared for weddings, Eid, and occasions where nothing less than the most impressive food will do. The dum cooking technique — sealing the pot with dough or foil and cooking on the lowest possible heat — creates a self-contained aromatic chamber where the rice and meat exchange flavours for 30 minutes. The result, when the seal is broken at the table, releases a cloud of fragrance unlike anything else in Kenyan cooking.
ingredients: 1 kg beef or goat — bone-in pieces
Pinch of saffron soaked in 4 tbsp warm milk
2 tsp biryani masala or curry powder
Dough for sealing (flour + water) or foil
4 tbsp crispy fried onions — for layering
equipment: Large heavy pot with tight lid
steps: Marinate meat in yogurt, garlic, ginger, biryani masala, turmeric, and salt for 1 hour.
Fry onions in ghee for 20—25 minutes until deeply golden. Reserve half for layering.
In the same pot, cook the marinated meat with the remaining fried onions and tomatoes for 30—35 minutes until almost tender.
Par-cook rice: boil in well-salted water with whole spices for 6—7 minutes until 70% cooked. Drain.
Layer the biryani: spread cooked meat at the base. Layer par-cooked rice over the meat.
Drizzle saffron milk over the rice. Sprinkle rose water if using.
Scatter mint, coriander, fried onions, and hard-boiled egg halves over the rice.
Seal the pot tightly — either press dough around the lid rim or seal completely with foil.
Cook on the absolute lowest heat for 30—35 minutes (dum stage).
Remove from heat. Rest sealed for 15 minutes.
Break the seal at the table for the full dramatic effect. Fold gently from the bottom to serve.
chefTips: The dum seal is the heart of biryani — once sealed, do not open until resting time is complete.
Par-cook rice only 70% — it will finish in the dum stage. Fully cooked rice becomes mushy.
The deepest-caramelised onions go into the meat layer; the second batch goes on top of the rice.
A heavy, thick-bottomed pot is essential — thin pots create hot spots and burn the base.
commonMistakes: Fully cooking the rice before layering.
Opening the pot during the dum stage.
Insufficient sealing — steam escaping ruins the dum effect.
recipes.storage: Refrigerate for up to 2 days — biryani is best eaten fresh.
recipes.reheating: Sprinkle with water and reheat in a sealed pot or microwave covered.
healthBenefits: Complete protein from meat.
Saffron provides crocin — a powerful antioxidant.
One-pot efficiency means less processing loss of nutrients.
recipes.culturalNote: Swahili biryani is the pinnacle of Kenyan coastal celebration cooking — the dish that signals a wedding, a major Eid feast, or a gathering of great importance. In Mombasa and Lamu, a skilled biryani cook is held in the highest esteem, and family biryani recipes are closely guarded and passed through generations.
regionalVariations: Mombasa biryani — the classic version.
Lamu biryani — more fragrant with extra rose water.
Chicken Swahili biryani — see KEN067.
Vegetable biryani — see KEN098.

faqs.q: What makes Swahili biryani different from Indian biryani?
faqs.a: Swahili biryani incorporates East African coastal influences — more tomatoes in the meat base, the use of whole coastal spices, and often rose water for fragrance. It is generally slightly less hot than South Asian biryanis and has a more pronounced caramelised onion flavour.

faqs.q: Is this suitable for a beginner?
faqs.a: Biryani requires patience and attention to detail at several stages. It is marked Hard difficulty — start with Chicken Pilau (KEN062) to understand the base technique before attempting this.

recipes.cookingScience: Dum cooking creates a closed thermodynamic system. The sealed pot traps steam from the meat and rice, which circulates continuously — cooking the rice gently from above and below simultaneously while the flavour compounds from the meat migrate upward into the rice layers. The dough seal (traditionally used) is more effective than foil as it creates a truly airtight environment.
sustainabilityTips: Biryani is the ultimate one-pot celebration meal — feeding 8—10 people from a single cooking session.

recipes.title: Kenyan Vegetable Pilau
recipes.community: Popular in urban Kenyan households — ideal for vegetarians
recipes.description: Kenyan Vegetable Pilau — fragrant basmati rice cooked with deeply caramelised onions, whole pilau spices, and a colourful mix of carrots, peas, and potatoes. All the aromatic celebration character of classic pilau, completely plant-based.
recipes.longDescription: Vegetable pilau proves that the magic of Kenyan pilau lies entirely in the technique — the deeply caramelised onions, the whole spices, the stock — not in the meat. Replace the meat with hearty vegetables and you get something equally aromatic, equally satisfying, and accessible to everyone at the table. It has become a staple in urban Kenyan homes where vegetarian cooking is increasingly popular.
ingredients: 2 cups (400g) basmati rice — rinsed and soaked 30 minutes
steps: Heat oil in a large pot. Cook onions for 18—20 minutes until deeply golden — the same caramelisation as meat pilau.
Add whole spices. Fry 1 minute.
Add garlic and ginger. Cook 1 minute.
Add tomatoes and turmeric. Cook for 8 minutes until thick.
Add carrots and potatoes. Stir and cook for 3 minutes.
Add drained rice, peas, and bell pepper. Stir once to combine.
Add vegetable stock. Bring to a boil.
Reduce to lowest heat. Cover tightly and cook undisturbed for 20 minutes.
Rest covered for 10 minutes. Fluff and garnish with coriander.
chefTips: Deeply caramelised onions are as important here as in meat pilau — 18—20 minutes minimum.
Add peas and bell pepper with the rice — they are delicate and need only the residual heat.
Use a good vegetable stock rather than plain water — the flavour difference is significant.
commonMistakes: Under-caramelising the onions — the pilau will taste flat.
Overcooking the vegetables — they should have some texture.
recipes.storage: Refrigerate for up to 3 days. Freeze for up to 2 months.
recipes.reheating: Sprinkle with water and reheat gently.
healthBenefits: High in dietary fibre from the variety of vegetables.
Complex carbohydrates from rice and potatoes.
Rich in vitamins A and C from carrots and peppers.
Completely plant-based and cholesterol-free.
recipes.culturalNote: Vegetable pilau has emerged as an important dish in modern Kenyan cooking — honouring the celebrated technique of the Swahili pilau tradition while making it accessible to vegetarians and those seeking lighter celebration food.
regionalVariations: Classic vegetable pilau.
Spicy vegetable pilau.
Coconut vegetable pilau — coastal style.
Lentil pilau — with red lentils for extra protein.

faqs.q: What other vegetables can I add?
faqs.a: Courgette, green beans, baby corn, and mushrooms all work well. Add them with the rice for the best texture.

recipes.cookingScience: Vegetables release steam during the covered cooking phase that contributes to cooking the rice from above. Root vegetables like carrots and potatoes are added earlier because their denser cell structure requires more heat to soften than the rice or delicate peas.
sustainabilityTips: Vegetable pilau has a significantly lower carbon footprint than meat pilau.
Use seasonal local vegetables for the most sustainable version.

recipes.title: Kenyan Coconut Pilau
recipes.community: Swahili — a coastal celebration speciality
recipes.description: Kenyan Coconut Pilau — the most fragrant of all Kenyan pilau variations. Basmati rice and spiced chicken or goat cooked in a blend of coconut milk and stock with whole coastal spices and deeply caramelised onions. Sweet, creamy, and aromatic — a coastal celebration in every grain.
recipes.longDescription: Coconut pilau takes the revered Mombasa pilau technique and adds the coast's other great ingredient — thick coconut milk — to the cooking liquid.
